body_markdown:
As thousands of students begin university life across the South East, first-year students are being encouraged to take up an NHS offer of free meningitis B vaccinations on campus.


The vaccination programme is being delivered during the busy start-of-term period, with pop-up clinics and pharmacy-led services being made available at universities including the University of Surrey, the University of Kent and the University of Chichester.


The campaign follows a serious meningitis B outbreak in Kent earlier this year, in which more than 20 young people, many of them students, became infected. All those affected required hospital treatment, while nine people were admitted to intensive care and two sadly died.


## Why are university freshers being offered the vaccine?


Starting university can mean living in shared accommodation, attending large social events and spending more time in close contact with other people.


According to NHS information cited in the supplied report, first-year university students have a substantially higher risk of developing meningococcal disease than young people of a similar age who are not attending university.


Meningococcal disease can develop quickly and can lead to serious illnesses including meningitis and sepsis. Although cases and outbreaks are uncommon, health authorities warn that the consequences can be severe.


The current MenB vaccination programme is intended to provide additional protection to eligible young people entering university.


The South East has recorded the highest number of MenB vaccinations under the temporary programme, with almost 50,000 students reported to have received a dose since the scheme began in July.


## Vaccination clinics are being held on university campuses


One of the main aims of the campaign is to make vaccination as straightforward as possible for students.


Rather than requiring students to arrange appointments far from campus, NHS England has commissioned community pharmacies to provide vaccination clinics at universities and other convenient locations.


The University of Surrey was among the institutions hosting a clinic during Freshers Week. Students were able to receive their vaccinations while taking part in the activities and events surrounding the start of the academic year.


Students at other universities in the region are also being encouraged to check their eligibility and find out when vaccination appointments are available.


The University of Kent, for example, has advised students to establish whether they are eligible for the MenB vaccine and to check whether they have previously received a first dose.


The university has also been offering walk-in opportunities and bookable appointments during October.


## Students encouraged to start the course early


The MenB vaccination programme involves two doses.


The doses need to be administered at least 28 days apart, meaning students who have not yet started the course are being encouraged to arrange their first vaccination as soon as possible.


Under the temporary programme described in the supplied report, the first dose needs to be given by 31 December 2026. Second doses can then be provided until 31 March 2027.


Starting the course early can therefore give students more time to complete the recommended schedule within the programme period.


Students who believe they have already received one dose should check their vaccination records rather than automatically assuming they need to start again.


## Why awareness of meningitis symptoms matters


Vaccination is only one part of protecting students from serious illness.


Health organisations are also urging young people to learn about the symptoms of meningitis and meningococcal disease and to look out for friends who may become unwell.


This is particularly relevant during university life, when tiredness, headaches, nausea and feeling generally unwell can easily be attributed to late nights, alcohol, stress or the demands of studying.


The Meningitis Research Foundation has highlighted the importance of recognising when symptoms could be more serious.


Symptoms associated with meningitis or meningococcal disease can include a severe headache, fever, vomiting, confusion, unusual sleepiness, sensitivity to light, a stiff neck and a rash that does not fade when pressed.


Symptoms do not necessarily appear in a particular order, and not everyone will experience every symptom.


Because meningococcal disease can progress rapidly, students who are seriously unwell should seek urgent medical attention rather than assuming their symptoms are simply the result of a hangover or exhaustion.


## The importance of looking after friends


University students are often surrounded by large groups of people, particularly during Freshers Week.


That makes looking out for friends an important part of staying safe.


Students may be more likely to notice changes in a friend's behaviour or appearance before the person who is ill realises how serious their symptoms could be.


Health campaigners are therefore encouraging students to familiarise themselves with meningitis symptoms and to take concerns seriously.


Knowing the signs does not mean that every headache or fever is meningitis. However, understanding the symptoms can help students recognise when professional medical advice or emergency assistance may be needed.


## Universities continue to support vaccination efforts


Several universities across the South East are working with NHS organisations and pharmacists to make the vaccination programme accessible to students.


Canterbury Christ Church University has said it is working with the NHS and pharmacists to arrange pop-up clinics at its Canterbury and Medway campuses.


The University of Sussex has also provided incoming UK students with NHS vaccination guidance and information about booking appointments. The university said it would continue working with public health partners and support students who require a second dose.


These arrangements reflect a broader effort to reach young people in places where they already spend much of their time.


For students, checking university emails, student health information and NHS guidance can help clarify whether they are eligible and where they can receive their vaccination.


## What students should do next


Students who are eligible for the MenB programme should check their vaccination history and find out how to access the service available through their university or local pharmacy.


Those who have not received a first dose may need to arrange one before the programme's December deadline.


Students who have already had a first dose should check when their second dose is due. The recommended interval between doses is at least 28 days.


It is also worth keeping a record of vaccination dates, particularly for students moving between university, home and healthcare services.


The NHS and participating universities can provide the most up-to-date information about eligibility, appointments and vaccination arrangements.


## A timely reminder for new students


The start of university is an exciting period, but it can also involve significant changes to daily routines, accommodation and social life.


The MenB vaccination campaign gives eligible students an opportunity to take an additional step towards protecting themselves against a rare but potentially serious disease.


The campaign is particularly significant in the South East following the meningitis B outbreak linked to a Canterbury nightclub earlier this year.


While outbreaks of meningococcal disease remain uncommon, the experience has highlighted why awareness, vaccination and prompt action when someone becomes seriously ill remain important.


For students beginning their university journey, checking vaccination status is a relatively simple task that can be completed alongside the many other preparations for the new academic year.


Students should check official NHS and university information to determine whether they are eligible for the MenB vaccination and how to arrange their doses.


### Disclaimer


This article is intended for general information and educational purposes only. Vaccination eligibility, availability and arrangements can change, so students should consult official NHS or university guidance for the latest information. Anyone experiencing potentially serious symptoms should seek appropriate medical attention promptly.
